*Part 3 of HOPE Under the Microscope*

A data-free method still needs a model of the data.

In HOPE, some of that model is already inside a trained BatchNorm checkpoint.
Each normalized channel carries a running mean and variance accumulated during
training. Those numbers are real information about the signals the network
once saw.

But they are not the whole distribution. They do not record how channels move
together. They do not record skewness, heavy tails, multimodality, spatial
dependence, or class-conditional structure. And they do not prove that a
trained feature direction is Gaussian.

HOPE bridges that gap with a Gaussian surrogate. This is the right place to be
precise about the phrase "data-free":

> Data-free is not assumption-free. The checkpoint supplies per-channel
> running means and variances; the surrogate supplies the unobserved
> distributional structure needed by the analytical kernel.

That distinction does not make the surrogate useless. It tells us what must be
tested.

This article is bound to
[arXiv:2607.21366v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366v1). The exact 70-page
PDF fingerprint is recorded in the
[paper manifest](https://github.com/basharelnashef/hope-under-the-microscope/blob/v1.0.0/paper/manifest.json).
The exact anchors are physical PDF pages 2, 6, 7, 52, 53, and 55; Eq. 83 on
page 55 supplies the exact biased pair moment used by the diagnostic. The
paper traceability summary above separates the paper's statements from the
algebra and diagnostics developed here.

## Evidence labels used here

This article uses four labels deliberately:

- `paper_claim`: what the paper says.
- `verified_fact`: algebra proved independently here, or a checkpoint fact
  backed by a frozen audit.
- `independent_inference`: our interpretation of stated premises.
- `open_question`: something neither the source nor the current evidence
  resolves.

The empirical checkpoint audit is frozen. Its measurements are a
`verified_fact` about one declared VGG-8 checkpoint and sample, not a universal
Gaussian-fit verdict.

## The strongest fair reading of HOPE's idea

`paper_claim` - HOPE needs expectations such as

$$
K(i,j)=
\mathbb E\left[
\operatorname{ReLU}(Y_i)\operatorname{ReLU}(Y_j)
\right]
$$

to compare the functions computed by neurons. If the original training data
are unavailable, those expectations cannot be evaluated directly over the
true layer-input distribution.

The paper's answer is not to pretend that no distribution is needed. Section
4 explicitly says the true input law is inaccessible and constructs a
surrogate. For a BatchNorm network, the checkpoint already contains empirical
constraints on each raw preactivation. HOPE uses those constraints to choose a
continuous Gaussian model, then evaluates the required ReLU moments
analytically.

This is an appealing computational exchange:

```text
stored moments + distributional model -> analytical expectations
```

It avoids repeatedly passing a dataset through the network during progressive
encoding. It also makes the assumptions inspectable. That is stronger than a
black-box score, provided we keep the stored evidence and the added model
separate.

On PDF page 2, the paper calls the method data-free for networks with
BatchNorm. Footnote 1 immediately gives the scope qualifier: architectures
without BatchNorm require a one-time calibration pass on a small data batch.
So even in the paper's own terminology, "data-free" describes the evaluation
procedure available for a particular kind of checkpoint. It does not mean
that the checkpoint contains no trace of its training distribution, and it
does not mean distribution-free.

## What BatchNorm actually stores

Consider one layer. Flatten the input patch to a vector
$X\in\mathbb R^n$, and collect the current raw channel weights as rows of
$W\in\mathbb R^{c\times n}$. In the bias-free model used for this
derivation, the raw preactivation vector is

$$
Z=WX.
$$

For each channel $i$, BatchNorm keeps a running mean $\mu_i$ and running
variance $\sigma_i^2$. In an idealized stationary setting where those
values equal exact moments under the same current map,

$$
\mu_i=\mathbb E[w_i^\top X],
\qquad
\sigma_i^2=\operatorname{Var}(w_i^\top X).
$$

Equivalently, with input mean $m_X$ and covariance $\Sigma_X$,

$$
Wm_X=\mu_{\mathrm{BN}},
\qquad
w_i^\top\Sigma_Xw_i=\sigma_i^2.
$$

`paper_claim` - These are the constraints that Section 4 uses to construct one
shared surrogate for a layer.

They are useful. The mean constraint locates the center as seen through each
trained filter. The variance constraint measures the scale of each raw
projection. After the learned BatchNorm affine transformation, those moments
lead to the effective preactivation parameters used in the self-kernel.

But notice the shape of the information: one mean and one variance per scalar
projection. BatchNorm observes a collection of one-dimensional shadows.

## What BatchNorm does not store

Suppose two channels have centered raw preactivations $Z_i$ and $Z_j$.
Knowing

$$
\mathbb E[Z_i],\quad \operatorname{Var}(Z_i),\quad
\mathbb E[Z_j],\quad \operatorname{Var}(Z_j)
$$

does not give

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Z_i,Z_j).
$$

Nor does it determine the joint distribution. Separate marginals can be
coupled in many ways.

`verified_fact` - Let $U$ and $V$ be independent standard normal random
variables. Compare three pairs:

$$
(U,U),\qquad (U,-U),\qquad (U,V).
$$

Every coordinate in all three pairs is standard normal. Each channel
therefore has the same mean, variance, and ReLU self-energy:

$$
\mathbb E[\operatorname{ReLU}(U)^2]=\frac12.
$$

Yet the ReLU cross-moment is

$$
\frac12,\qquad 0,\qquad \frac{1}{2\pi},
$$

respectively. Identical one-dimensional marginals can support maximally
aligned, anti-aligned, or independent pair behavior.

This is not a claim that any of those three toy couplings is the trained
network's joint distribution. It is a proof of non-identifiability: separate
channel statistics alone cannot tell us which dependence is present.

That boundary matters because HOPE uses both kinds of quantities:

- The self-kernel $K(i,i)$ depends only on one channel's marginal.
- The pair kernel $K(i,j)$ depends on a joint law.

BatchNorm can support the first more directly than the second.

## A marginal Gaussian is enough for the self-kernel

After BatchNorm and its learned affine transform, write

$$
Y_i=
\frac{\gamma_i}{\sqrt{\sigma_i^2+\epsilon}}
(w_i^\top X-\mu_i)+\beta_i.
$$

If the stored moments agree with the moments of the current raw projection,
then

$$
\mathbb E[Y_i]=\beta_i
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=
\gamma_i^2
\frac{\sigma_i^2}{\sigma_i^2+\epsilon}.
$$

`paper_claim` - Eq. 77 prints the finite-epsilon variance. The text then takes
epsilon to be negligible and Eq. 78 writes

$$
Y_i\sim\mathcal N(\beta_i,\gamma_i^2).
$$

Under that scalar Gaussian premise, the ReLU self-kernel is a
one-dimensional truncated-normal moment. Appendix E.2 evaluates it in closed
form:

$$
K(i,i)=
(\gamma_i^2+\beta_i^2)
\Phi\left(\frac{\beta_i}{|\gamma_i|}\right)
+
\beta_i|\gamma_i|
\phi\left(\frac{\beta_i}{|\gamma_i|}\right).
$$

Part 2 independently verified this identity under its stated marginal model.
Part 3 asks the upstream question: how well does that marginal model describe
captured checkpoint preactivations?

The distinction is important. A poor empirical fit would not make the integral
wrong. It would show that its premise is a poor approximation for the
evaluated channel and sample. A close fit would support the approximation in
that bounded setting, not establish a universal theorem.

## A pair kernel needs dependence too

The cross-kernel is

$$
K(i,j)=
\mathbb E[
\operatorname{ReLU}(Y_i)
\operatorname{ReLU}(Y_j)
].
$$

Even if both scalar marginals are exactly Gaussian, this expectation remains
undetermined until their dependence is specified. Under a bivariate Gaussian
model, a correlation parameter completes the pair law. But BatchNorm does not
store that correlation.

`paper_claim` - Section 4 proposes a shared maximum-entropy covariance under
the per-channel variance constraints, then says that practical pairwise
operations bypass the full high-dimensional covariance. Appendix E develops
the pair construction.

Part 3 stops at the information boundary: the dependence is reconstructed, not
read directly from separate BatchNorm buffers. Whether the entropy problem is
well-posed belongs to Part 4. Whether separately constructed pair kernels form
one global positive-semidefinite Gram matrix belongs to Part 5.

This separation prevents one valid criticism from being stretched into a
different claim. "BatchNorm does not identify the joint law" is exact. "The
paper's selected joint surrogate is wrong on every network" is not established.

## What the Gaussianity argument does and does not prove

`paper_claim` - On PDF page 6, HOPE gives a two-step motivation.

First, a neuron observes a high-dimensional input through a scalar weighted
sum. The paper invokes the Central Limit Theorem and the Diaconis-Freedman
effect to argue that high-fan-in preactivations become Gaussian. It adds that
although ReLU disrupts Gaussianity, later high-dimensional linear maps smooth
the signal back toward Gaussian preactivations.

Second, it chooses a multivariate Gaussian input surrogate because every
linear combination of a multivariate Gaussian is Gaussian. In the
"Post-ReLU Support Paradox" box, it argues that the kernel depends only on a
two-dimensional preactivation slice, so replacing the nonnegative ambient
post-ReLU support can remain asymptotically accurate.

This is a coherent motivation. It is not itself a measurement; the frozen
checkpoint audit below supplies one bounded empirical test.

`independent_inference` - Central-limit intuition has conditions. Contributions
must not be dominated by a small number of terms, and their dependence must be
controlled. Typical-projection results concern most or randomly oriented
directions under their hypotheses. A trained filter is not drawn independently
of the data. Optimization selects directions that detect structure.

Modern convolutional layers add concrete reasons to measure rather than
assume:

- a receptive field can be small;
- neighboring spatial values can be strongly correlated;
- post-ReLU inputs can be sparse and asymmetric;
- a few weights can dominate a projection;
- mixtures of classes or activation regimes can remain multimodal;
- early, middle, and late layers need not behave alike.

None of these bullets proves non-Gaussianity. Together they explain why an
asymptotic story should be checked in the actual trained directions used by
the method.

`open_question` - For a fixed checkpoint and sample, which channels are close
enough to the Gaussian surrogate for the resulting kernel estimates, and
which are not?

## Eq. 76: the width objection that does not work

The review history matters here because an initially tempting criticism was
wrong.

On PDF page 7, HOPE defines the layer surrogate mean as

$$
\widehat\mu_X=W^+\mu_{\mathrm{BN}}.
$$

Appendix E.1 then uses

$$
W\widehat\mu_X=WW^+\mu_{\mathrm{BN}}=\mu_{\mathrm{BN}}
$$

to obtain Eq. 76.

The equality holds exactly when $\mu_{\mathrm{BN}}$ lies in the column space of
$W$, because $WW^+$ is the orthogonal projector onto that space.

It can look as if an expanding layer, with more output channels than input
coordinates, should make an arbitrary $\mu_{\mathrm{BN}}$ miss that subspace. But
the relevant vector is not arbitrary. Under the same bias-free linear model,

$$
\mu_{\mathrm{BN}}=\mathbb E[WX]=W\mathbb E[X].
$$

It is therefore in the column space by construction, independent of whether
the layer expands or contracts.

`verified_fact` - Width alone does not break Eq. 76.

That conclusion must survive every rewrite of Part 3. A synthetic
counterexample that samples $W$ and $\mu_{\mathrm{BN}}$ independently violates
the premise it claims to test.

Real checkpoints can still depart from the ideal equality. Running statistics
are exponential moving averages accumulated while weights change. A raw
affine bias might be omitted from the equation. The extraction graph might not
match the algebra. Convolutional spatial aggregation can import a stationarity
approximation. Numerical conditioning also matters.

Those are hypotheses about causes, not automatic findings. The audit should
measure the normalized projection residual

$$
R_\mu=
\frac{\lVert(I-WW^+)\mu_{\mathrm{BN}}\rVert_2}
{\max(\lVert\mu_{\mathrm{BN}}\rVert_2,\tau)}
$$

with a declared floor $\tau$, then report what happens for the specified
checkpoint. It must not relabel a residual as a width failure.

## The frozen checkpoint audit

`P03-CHECKPOINT-GAUSSIAN-DIAGNOSTIC` is a bounded composite claim record from
one VGG-8/CIFAR-10 `architecture_adaptation`. Its raw checkpoint measurements
and algebraic decomposition identities are `verified_fact`; its interpretation
of Gaussian-surrogate fit errors is `independent_inference`. The exact
checkpoint fingerprint is recorded in the
[frozen summary](https://github.com/basharelnashef/hope-under-the-microscope/blob/v1.0.0/artifacts/part_03/results/summary.json).

The audit used 2,000 CIFAR-10 test examples selected by a sorted, seeded,
near-equal class-stratified sample without replacement. The selected-example
fingerprint is recorded in the same frozen summary.

It captured 16 deterministic channels and eight pairs at each graph point:

| Layer | Module | Shape and rank | Observations |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `conv0` | `features.1` | 128 by 27, rank 27 | 32,000 |
| `conv2` | `features.9` | 512 by 2,304, rank 512 | 32,000 |
| `conv5` | `features.19` | 512 by 4,608, rank 512 | 32,000 |
| `dense` | `bn_b` | 512 by 512, rank 512 | 2,000 |

`conv0` selected channels 0, 8, 16, 25, 33, 42, 50, 59, 67, 76, 84, 93,
101, 110, 118, and 127. Each other graph point selected channels 0, 34, 68,
102, 136, 170, 204, 238, 272, 306, 340, 374, 408, 442, 476, and 511.

The full channel lists, selection rules, output fingerprints, and configuration
fingerprint are recorded in the frozen summary.
The [artifact checksum index](https://github.com/basharelnashef/hope-under-the-microscope/blob/v1.0.0/artifacts/SHA256SUMS)
authenticates the published result files.

The checkpoint's historical training provenance is incomplete. Its bytes and
strict-loaded state schema are bound, but epoch history, optimizer and
scheduler state, training-data hashes, and the original generating command
and environment are unavailable. The audit uses no legacy compression result
and does not reproduce HOPE's ResNet-50/ImageNet experiment.

### What the selected one-dimensional distributions looked like

Across the four layer-summary rows, per-layer median absolute skewness ranged
from `0.4381046015109638` to `0.916664923200222`; the largest selected-channel
value was `2.3082733334908636`. Median absolute excess kurtosis ranged from
`0.5276760976728814` to `4.1728378058823345`, with maximum
`9.07941365824211`. Median fitted-normal KS distance ranged from
`0.04980412829317285` to `0.13194043073030828`, with maximum
`0.2124892081316252`.

Those values show substantial variation across the selected channels. They do
not produce one network-wide yes-or-no Gaussian label. Spatial positions and
repeated values from each image are correlated, so these are descriptive
effect sizes, not normality p-values.

### Separating three self-kernel errors

Let $G(m,s)$ denote the exact Gaussian ReLU second moment. The audit compares
the empirical moment $E_i$, a Gaussian fitted to captured moments
$G_i^{\mathrm{emp}}$, the checkpoint prediction with finite epsilon
$G_i^{\mathrm{BN},\epsilon}$, and the paper's negligible-epsilon prediction
$G_i^{\mathrm{BN},0}$. The signed error telescopes:

$$
E_i-G_i^{\mathrm{BN},0}
=
\underbrace{E_i-G_i^{\mathrm{emp}}}_{\text{shape}}
+
\underbrace{G_i^{\mathrm{emp}}-G_i^{\mathrm{BN},\epsilon}}_{\text{moment state}}
+
\underbrace{G_i^{\mathrm{BN},\epsilon}-G_i^{\mathrm{BN},0}}_{\text{finite epsilon}}.
$$

Across the four layer summaries, median Gaussian-fit self-kernel absolute error
ranged from `0.00013562328773035452` to `0.001469023748179522`; the largest
selected absolute error was `0.008144367516825735`. Median bounded symmetric
error ranged from `0.018853763884460188` to `0.5458623797033268`.
Near-dead channels reached the symmetric metric ceiling `2.0`, so that ceiling
must be read beside the small absolute-error scale.

The decomposition identity is a fail-closed gate. The sizes of the Gaussian
fit errors are not pass gates; they are the scientific observations.

### Pair moments and dependence

Across 32 selected pairs, the empirical-versus-exact-biased-Gaussian absolute
error ranged from `3.222170944350448e-10` to `0.007075261127352704`.
Bounded symmetric error ranged from `0.000633394514674313` to `2.0`, again with
near-zero pair moments at the ceiling.

Independently shuffling one channel preserved the measured marginal summaries
to maximum absolute difference `5.551115123125783e-17`, while per-layer scaled
dependence change ranged from `0.2981947166796576` to
`0.6397540775253039`. The shuffle is an identifiability diagnostic, not a
plausible replacement network distribution.

### What Eq. 76 measured

The 128 by 27 rank-27 `conv0` expansion had the only nontrivial stored-mean
projection residual: `0.000551072218291825`. It measures mismatch with the
ideal current common-map condition. It does not show that expansion width
caused the mismatch.

The other maps were full row rank. Their column spaces equal their output
spaces, so machine-scale residuals from `1.0827529949270106e-15` to
`1.4707953601090622e-15` are non-diagnostic: any stored mean vector projects
back in those cases. They do not prove that running statistics are current.

The separate same-sample common-map residual ranged from
`5.718194556149604e-10` to `1.1232923462430606e-8`, and all four declared
implementation gates passed. That supports the implementation of the ideal
algebra without converting width into a causal explanation.

### The bounded conclusion

The selected channels do not share one uniform Gaussian-fit profile. Some
absolute ReLU-moment errors are small while normalized errors saturate on
near-dead signals; pair behavior also changes when marginals are held fixed.
This is evidence about the declared specimen and estimands. It is not
"neural preactivations are Gaussian" or "HOPE's Gaussian premise is false."

Whether these discrepancies change pruning or merge rankings remains an
`open_question`.

## So what does data-free mean here?

`independent_inference` - For a BatchNorm checkpoint, HOPE can compute its
surrogate-based scores without loading real or synthetic examples during the
encoding loop. That is a meaningful operational advantage.

But the computation still depends on:

1. historical moments stored from training;
2. an idealized relationship between those moments and current weights;
3. a Gaussian marginal premise;
4. a reconstructed dependence model for pair operations;
5. architectural assumptions about the observed projections and graph.

The better phrase is not "no data model." It is "a checkpoint-carried,
analytically completed data model."

That description is both fairer and more useful. It shows why the method can
be efficient, why BatchNorm is central, where calibration enters without
BatchNorm, and where empirical validation should focus.

## What the audit establishes

Several conclusions now have frozen support.

`paper_claim` - HOPE intentionally replaces the inaccessible true layer-input
distribution with a Gaussian surrogate constrained by BatchNorm statistics.

`verified_fact` - BatchNorm's separate channel means and variances do not
identify cross-channel dependence or a full joint distribution.

`verified_fact` - The Eq. 76 mean reconstruction is exact under one common
bias-free linear model. Width alone is not a counterexample.

`independent_inference` - CLT and typical-projection intuition motivate a
surrogate but do not substitute for measurement in trained directions.

`verified_fact` - On the declared VGG-8 checkpoint and sample, the bounded raw
measurements, exact self-kernel decomposition identities, shuffle-preserved
marginals, and Eq. 76 projection measurements are as reported above.

`independent_inference` - The measured marginal-shape, self-kernel, and
pair-kernel discrepancies quantify fit to the chosen Gaussian surrogate; their
variation by layer and signal scale does not by itself establish behavior for
other checkpoints or the paper's target architecture.

`open_question` - Are any measured errors large enough to alter HOPE's action
rankings, and do the patterns transfer to other checkpoints?

The final question is the constructive one. Data-free methods do not need to
hide their assumptions. They can expose them, test them on provenance-bound
checkpoints, and report exactly where analytical convenience remains faithful
to the learned signals.

That is the standard Part 3 applies.
